name: Paeonol

lead: Paeonol is a small phenolic molecule from peony root bark, long used in traditional Chinese medicine.
In skincare circles it is discussed as a plant-derived option for brightening and reducing pigmentation, and it also appears in research for anti-inflammatory effects.

paras: Paeonol is reported to be anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and weakly active on MAO enzymes; in lab studies it has been explored for effects on pigment-producing pathways.
Human data are limited. A phase 2 trial of a paeonol-containing combination was run in knee osteoarthritis. As with any botanical-derived topical, individual sensitivity can vary.

chain: Aimed at a more even, brighter complexion
angle.text: Paeonol is used as a plant-derived skincare ingredient aimed at calming redness and evening tone, working through anti-inflammatory and antioxidant properties described in laboratory research. Appearance-specific human trials have not been published; the clinical work concerns joint, heart and mouth conditions.

lead: Paeonol (2'-hydroxy-4'-methoxyacetophenone) is a small phenolic compound found in the root bark of the tree peony (Paeonia suffruticosa, the moutan cortex of traditional Chinese medicine) and in other plants such as Arisaema erubescens and Dioscorea japonica.[1][2] It is the main active component attributed to moutan cortex, a herb used in East Asian medicine for thousands of years.[3][4]

For appearance, paeonol is mentioned as a plant-derived ingredient in skin-brightening and tone-evening products, where the idea is that a peony-derived phenolic with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties may calm irritation and support a more even-looking complexion.[2] The published literature itself is mostly pharmacological: reviews describe anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, anti-atherosclerotic and neuroprotective actions, largely in cells and animals.[2][3][5][4]

Human studies include a phase 2a trial of an apocynin and paeonol combination in knee osteoarthritis, a trial of a paeonol-containing pill in unstable angina and a herbal-formula trial in dry mouth.[6][7][8] Paeonol injection has been used in China for roughly 50 years for inflammation and pain indications, according to a pharmacology review.[4]

paras: Paeonol is an O-methylated phenol and aromatic ketone with the formula C9H10O3 and a molar mass near 166 g/mol.[1] It occurs in Paeonia suffruticosa and in other medicinal plants including Cynanchum paniculatum and Paeonia lactiflora.[1][2] Medicinal-chemistry reviews describe many synthetic paeonol derivatives made to modify its antibacterial, anti-inflammatory, analgesic and antioxidant activity.[2] A cancer-focused review notes that paeonol itself is described as having poor stability, low bioavailability and a short half-life, and that nanomaterial delivery systems are being explored to address this.[9]

In rats, paeonol dose-dependently reduced carrageenan-induced thermal hyperalgesia and lowered TNF-alpha and IL-1beta formation.[10] Reviews describe antiplatelet, anti-atherosclerotic, antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects and protective effects in models of stroke, Alzheimer's and Parkinson's disease.[3][5] Reviews of anticancer work describe effects on cell proliferation and apoptosis in cell and animal models.[9] Wikipedia reports weak inhibition of monoamine oxidases A and B in vitro.[1] Paeonol has also been reported to ease colitis in mice through PPAR-gamma and NF-kappaB pathways.[11]
A 2012 study characterised paeonol metabolites in human urine.[12]

Paeonol and moutan bark extract appear in skincare descriptions as soothing and brightening ingredients drawn from traditional Chinese medicine. Proponents point to its anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions as relevant to redness, irritation and uneven tone. Published studies reviewed here examine these actions in other tissues, and no randomised trial of paeonol for skin pigmentation appears among them.

A multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial tested a fixed-dose combination of apocynin and paeonol (APPA) in people with radiographic knee osteoarthritis and WOMAC pain of at least 40 out of 100.[6] The registry lists a completed phase 2 study (NCT04657926) with 152 participants that began in September 2020, and a phase 1 study in healthy subjects and osteoarthritis patients that began in 2018.[13][14]

A randomised, double-blind trial of the Korean herbal formula Yukmijihwang-tang, which contains moutan cortex among its ingredients, examined dry mouth in elderly people.[7] A Chinese randomised trial of a compound paeonol dripping pill looked at plasma inflammatory mediators in unstable angina.[8] Neither studied skin tone.
Most other work is preclinical, covering atherosclerosis, central nervous system protection, colitis, lupus nephritis models and cancer.[3][5][9][11]

Published human trials are of specific combination products, so the safety information they report relates to those formulations. As with any botanical-derived ingredient applied to skin, individual sensitivity varies.

Paeonol is a standard marker compound for moutan cortex in Chinese medicine, and paeonol injections and other dosage forms have been used in China for inflammatory and pain-related indications.[4] Recent reviews also examine delivery platforms such as plant-derived extracellular vesicles for traditional Chinese medicine compounds including paeonol.[15]
